title: The arteries of the head and neck
summary: Two systems into the head: carotid in front for the face and forebrain, vertebral behind for the brainstem.
objectives: Trace the common carotid to its two divisions and name their territories
Explain what the vertebral arteries supply and how they get there
Say why the internal carotid gives no branch in the neck
Trace the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries as the two terminal external carotid branches
takeaways: External carotid supplies the face, scalp and neck; internal carotid supplies the brain and the eye.
The internal carotid has no branches in the neck — that is how you identify it at operation.
The vertebral arteries join to form the basilar and supply the posterior circulation.
The superficial temporal artery ascends towards the scalp; the maxillary artery turns deep into the infratemporal region.

steps.title: Two arteries up each side
steps.text:
Blood reaches the head by two routes. In front, the common carotid artery runs up in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve. Behind, the vertebral artery climbs through the foramina transversaria of the cervical vertebrae.

On the right both come from the brachiocephalic trunk; on the left the common carotid comes directly from the arch and the vertebral from the subclavian.

check.q: Which two vessels bring blood to the head, and where does each run?
check.a: Common carotid in the carotid sheath anteriorly, vertebral artery through the foramina transversaria posteriorly.

steps.title: The bifurcation
steps.text:
At the upper border of the thyroid cartilage — about C4 — the common carotid divides into external and internal branches. The dilatation at the origin of the internal carotid is the carotid sinus, a baroreceptor supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve; pressing on it slows the heart.

The bifurcation is also where atheroma collects, and where a plaque throws emboli into the brain or the eye. Carotid endarterectomy is performed exactly here.
steps.clinical: Amaurosis fugax — a curtain descending over one eye — is a carotid embolus to the retina, and a warning of stroke on the same side.

check.q: At what vertebral level does the common carotid usually divide?
check.a: C4, at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.

steps.title: The external carotid and its eight branches
steps.text:
The external carotid supplies everything outside the skull: face, scalp, mouth, nose and much of the neck. Its branches, from below up, are the superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, and then the two terminal branches, the maxillary and the superficial temporal.

Two are worth feeling for. The facial artery crosses the mandible at the anterior border of masseter — the facial pulse. The superficial temporal artery runs in front of the ear, and is the vessel biopsied in giant cell arteritis.
steps.mnemonic: Some Anatomists Like Freiburg, Others Prefer Simply Music: Superior thyroid, Ascending pharyngeal, Lingual, Facial, Occipital, Posterior auricular, Superficial temporal, Maxillary.

steps.title: The internal carotid
steps.text:
The internal carotid gives no branches in the neck at all. That single fact identifies it at surgery, and it is worth checking on the model.

It enters the carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone, runs an S-shaped course through the cavernous sinus — where it lies beside cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI — gives the ophthalmic artery to the eye, and finally divides into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

check.q: How can you tell the internal from the external carotid artery in the neck?
check.a: The internal carotid has no branches in the neck.

steps.title: The vertebral arteries and the posterior circulation
steps.text:
Each vertebral artery enters the foramen transversarium of C6, climbs to C1, turns horizontally across the posterior arch of the atlas, and passes through the foramen magnum. The two then join on the front of the pons as the basilar artery.

Between them they supply the cervical spinal cord, the brainstem, the cerebellum and the occipital lobes. So a posterior circulation stroke gives dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia and visual field loss rather than the hemiparesis of a carotid stroke.

check.q: At which vertebra does the vertebral artery enter the foramen transversarium?

steps.title: Where the two systems meet
steps.text:
At the base of the brain the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems are joined by the cerebral arterial circle — the circle of Willis — through the anterior and posterior communicating arteries.

In theory that means either system can supply the whole brain. In practice the circle is complete in fewer than half of people, and the communicating arteries are often too small to carry much. It is a better explanation of where aneurysms form than of how strokes are prevented.
steps.pitfall: Do not over-rely on the circle of Willis: it is anatomically complete in a minority, and collateral flow through it is often inadequate.

steps.title: The terminal branches take opposite depths
steps.text:
Within the parotid region, behind the neck of the mandible, the external carotid ends as the superficial temporal and maxillary arteries. The superficial temporal branch ascends in front of the ear, crossing the zygomatic arch to reach the scalp.

The maxillary artery turns deep into the infratemporal region and supplies structures including the teeth, deep face, nasal cavity and dura through its branches. The middle meningeal artery is one of those branches. Thus an external carotid pathway can supply intracranial dura even though the internal carotid is the major carotid supply to the brain itself.

check.q: Does the middle meningeal artery arise from the internal carotid simply because it enters the skull?
check.a: No. It usually arises from the maxillary artery, a terminal branch of the external carotid.

title: The dural venous sinuses
summary: Veins with no valves and no muscle, running between two layers of dura — and the routes infection takes into them.
objectives: Trace venous blood from the superior sagittal sinus to the internal jugular vein
List the structures in the wall and lumen of the cavernous sinus
Explain the danger area of the face
Relate the straight sinus to the drainage of the deep cerebral veins
takeaways: Superior sagittal → confluence → transverse → sigmoid → internal jugular vein.
Cavernous sinus wall: III, IV, V1, V2. Inside it: the internal carotid artery and VI.
The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus and has no valves.
The great cerebral vein joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus, linking deep cerebral drainage to the dural sinus system.

steps.title: What a dural sinus is
steps.text:
Not an ordinary vein. A dural venous sinus is a channel between the periosteal and meningeal layers of the dura, lined by endothelium but with rigid walls, no muscle and no valves.

Rigid walls mean the sinuses cannot collapse, which keeps venous drainage open whatever the intracranial pressure. No valves means blood can flow either way — which is how infection travels backwards into the skull.

steps.title: The main route
steps.text:
The superior sagittal sinus runs back along the upper attached border of the falx cerebri, collecting cerebral veins and, through the arachnoid granulations, cerebrospinal fluid. The inferior sagittal sinus runs in the free lower edge of the falx and joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus.

Both reach the confluence of sinuses at the internal occipital protuberance, and from there the transverse sinus runs forwards in the attached edge of the tentorium, becomes the sigmoid sinus as it curves down, and leaves by the jugular foramen as the internal jugular vein.

check.q: Trace blood from the vertex to the neck.
check.a: Superior sagittal sinus → confluence → transverse sinus → sigmoid sinus → internal jugular vein.

steps.title: The cavernous sinus
steps.text:
A plexus of veins either side of the body of the sphenoid, and the most crowded space in the head. In its lateral wall, from above down: the oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) nerves. Running through the lumen: the internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve (VI).

Because VI lies free in the blood stream beside the artery, it is the first nerve to suffer when the sinus is under pressure — an isolated abducens palsy is a warning sign here.
steps.mnemonic: O TOM CAT — in the wall: Oculomotor, Trochlear, Ophthalmic, Maxillary. Traversing the lumen: Carotid, Abducens.

check.q: Which two structures run through the cavity of the cavernous sinus rather than in its wall?
check.a: The internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve (VI).

steps.title: The danger area of the face
steps.text:
The facial vein drains the area around the nose and upper lip. Through the superior ophthalmic vein it communicates directly with the cavernous sinus — and, like all these veins, it has no valves.

So an infected lesion in the triangle between the corners of the mouth and the bridge of the nose can spread backwards into the sinus and cause a cavernous sinus thrombosis: a proptosed, congested, painful eye with an ophthalmoplegia and a very unwell patient. It is the reason this part of the face is treated with more respect than any other.
steps.clinical: Cavernous sinus thrombosis: chemosis, proptosis, painful ophthalmoplegia, fever — an emergency.

check.q: Why is the area around the upper lip and nose called the danger area?
check.a: The valveless facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins.

steps.title: Emissary veins and the bigger picture
steps.text:
Small emissary veins pass through the skull to connect the sinuses with veins of the scalp and face. They allow the same two-way traffic, and they also help cool the brain.

The same principle runs down the whole body: the valveless vertebral venous plexus connects the pelvic veins to the intracranial sinuses, which is one reason prostatic carcinoma metastasises to the spine and skull without passing through the lungs.

check.q: How can prostate cancer reach the vertebrae without going through the lungs?
check.a: Through the valveless vertebral venous plexus, which bypasses the caval system.

steps.title: The deep brain has its own collecting route
steps.text:
Superficial cerebral veins drain the cortex into nearby dural sinuses, but deep structures use a different collecting system. The paired internal cerebral veins contribute to the great cerebral vein, also called the vein of Galen, behind the splenium of the corpus callosum.

The great cerebral vein joins the inferior sagittal sinus to form the straight sinus, which runs at the junction of falx and tentorium towards the confluence region. Follow deep brain, deep veins, straight sinus, then the larger outflow route; not every cerebral vein drains first into the superior sagittal sinus.

check.q: Which two channels unite to form the straight sinus?
check.a: The great cerebral vein and the inferior sagittal sinus.

title: The arteries of the upper limb
summary: One vessel that changes its name four times, and the places you can feel it.
objectives: Follow the arterial supply from subclavian to the digital arteries
Name the pulse points of the upper limb and where to feel each
Explain the double supply to the hand and the Allen test
Explain how arterial anastomoses around the elbow link vessels above and below the joint
takeaways: Subclavian → axillary at the first rib → brachial at the lower border of teres major → radial and ulnar in the cubital fossa.
The superficial arch is mostly ulnar, the deep arch mostly radial.
Palmar collateral anatomy varies; adequacy of alternative hand perfusion must be assessed before radial artery sacrifice.
Descending collateral and ascending recurrent branches form elbow anastomoses; collateral routes do not guarantee adequate flow after an acute obstruction.

steps.title: One artery, four names
steps.text:
It is a single vessel with changing names at fixed landmarks. The subclavian artery becomes the axillary at the outer border of the first rib; the axillary becomes the brachial at the lower border of teres major; the brachial divides in the cubital fossa into radial and ulnar.

Each boundary is a bony or muscular landmark, which is what makes the naming useful: it tells you exactly where in the limb you are.

check.q: Where does the axillary artery become the brachial artery?
check.a: At the lower border of teres major.

steps.title: The axillary artery and its three parts
steps.text:
Pectoralis minor crosses the artery and divides it into three parts: the first part has one branch, the second two, the third three.

The third part's branches matter most: the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries, which encircle the surgical neck of the humerus with the axillary nerve, and the subscapular artery, the largest branch. Around the scapula these form an anastomosis good enough that the axillary artery can be ligated in its first part and the arm survive.

steps.title: The brachial artery
steps.text:
The brachial artery runs down the medial side of the arm with the median nerve crossing in front of it, and gives the deep brachial artery into the radial groove.

In the cubital fossa it lies medial to the biceps tendon and deep to the bicipital aponeurosis — which is why a blood pressure cuff works here, and why the aponeurosis protects the artery from a badly aimed needle in the antecubital fossa.

check.q: Where exactly do you place the stethoscope for a brachial blood pressure?
check.a: Medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.

steps.title: Radial and ulnar
steps.text:
The radial artery runs down the lateral forearm, superficial and easily felt against the distal radius, then dives through the anatomical snuffbox to the back of the hand and between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous into the palm.

The ulnar artery runs deep to the flexors, joins the ulnar nerve, and enters the hand superficial to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal — lateral to the pisiform, with the nerve on its medial side.

steps.title: Two arches in the hand
steps.text:
The superficial palmar arch is formed mainly by the ulnar artery and lies just deep to the palmar aponeurosis, at the level of the fully extended thumb. The deep palmar arch is formed mainly by the radial artery and lies a centimetre proximal to it, against the metacarpal bases.

The connected arches often provide collateral supply, but their completeness varies. In a modified Allen test, releasing the ulnar artery while keeping the radial compressed assesses reperfusion through the ulnar route. Failure to reperfuse suggests inadequate flow through the released artery and its connections, not proof that it is the sole supply. This bedside test has limitations; clinical assessment may use additional vascular tests.

check.q: Which artery mainly forms the superficial palmar arch?
check.a: The ulnar artery.

steps.title: Branches go down and come back up
steps.text:
Around the elbow, collateral branches descend from arteries above the joint and meet recurrent branches ascending from below it. The radial and ulnar sides each have such connections around the epicondyles.

These anastomoses provide alternative routes as joint position changes and may enlarge gradually when a main route narrows. They do not guarantee sufficient flow after a sudden interruption: vessel size, the level of obstruction and the time available to adapt all matter. A connected map shows possible routes, not an assurance that every route can carry the required volume.

check.q: What does recurrent mean in the name of an elbow artery?
check.a: It turns back towards the joint from an artery arising below it, to connect with descending collateral branches.

title: The arteries of the lower limb
summary: One line from the inguinal ligament to the toes, with three pulses you must be able to find.
objectives: Follow the external iliac artery to the foot and name the changes of name
Locate the femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses
Relate the level of an occlusion to the site of claudication
Separate continuity of a large artery from adequate tissue perfusion downstream
takeaways: External iliac → femoral under the inguinal ligament → popliteal at the adductor hiatus → anterior and posterior tibial below the knee.
Profunda femoris is the main supply of the thigh and the key collateral vessel.
Claudication is felt one joint below the block: buttock (aorto-iliac), thigh (common femoral), calf (superficial femoral).
A distal pulse reflects pressure waves in a patent artery; it does not by itself prove adequate capillary perfusion in every tissue compartment.

steps.title: The line of the artery
steps.text:
The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery as it passes under the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point — halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. That is where you feel the femoral pulse and where a femoral line goes in.

It runs down through the femoral triangle and the adductor canal, then passes through the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal artery behind the knee.
steps.mnemonic: NAVY in the femoral triangle, lateral to medial: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts.

check.q: Where do you feel the femoral pulse?
check.a: At the midinguinal point, halfway between the ASIS and the pubic symphysis, just below the inguinal ligament.

steps.title: Profunda femoris
steps.text:
A few centimetres below the inguinal ligament the femoral artery gives its largest branch, the deep femoral artery (profunda femoris), which supplies almost the whole thigh through its perforating branches, and gives the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries to the hip.

Because the profunda's perforators anastomose with the popliteal branches, it becomes the collateral route when the superficial femoral artery occludes. That is why a patient can have a completely blocked superficial femoral artery and still have a viable leg — with claudication.

steps.title: The popliteal artery and its danger
steps.text:
The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, lying directly on the capsule of the knee joint and tethered above and below.

That fixity is why it is injured in a posterior knee dislocation and in a displaced supracondylar femoral fracture, and why any knee dislocation demands vascular assessment. Around the joint it forms the genicular anastomosis, which is rarely enough on its own to save the leg.
steps.clinical: Any knee dislocation, even one that has spontaneously reduced, needs documented pulses and usually formal imaging.

check.q: Why is the popliteal artery so vulnerable in knee dislocation?
check.a: It lies directly on the joint capsule and is tethered at both ends, so it cannot move out of the way.

steps.title: Below the knee
steps.text:
The popliteal artery divides at the lower border of popliteus. The anterior tibial artery passes forwards through the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment and becomes the dorsalis pedis on the dorsum of the foot. The posterior tibial artery continues down the deep posterior compartment, gives the fibular artery, and passes behind the medial malleolus into the sole as the medial and lateral plantar arteries.

So the foot, like the hand, has a double supply — a dorsal and a plantar arch, connected by a perforating branch.

steps.title: Finding the pulses
steps.text:
Femoral: midinguinal point. Popliteal: deep in the fossa with the knee slightly flexed, pressing against the tibia — the hardest to find. Posterior tibial: a fingerbreadth behind and below the medial malleolus. Dorsalis pedis: on the dorsum, lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.

Dorsalis pedis is congenitally absent or unusually placed in about one person in ten, so a missing dorsalis pedis with a good posterior tibial pulse is usually anatomy rather than disease.

check.q: Where do you feel the dorsalis pedis pulse?
check.a: On the dorsum of the foot, immediately lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.

steps.title: Where it hurts tells you where it is blocked
steps.text:
Claudication is felt in the muscle group below the level of the obstruction, because that is the group whose supply cannot keep up with demand.

Buttock and thigh claudication with impotence and absent femoral pulses is aorto-iliac disease (Leriche syndrome). Thigh claudication points to the common femoral. Calf claudication — much the commonest — points to the superficial femoral artery, usually in the adductor canal.

check.q: Calf claudication with a normal femoral pulse. Where is the lesion?
check.a: The superficial femoral artery, typically in the adductor canal.

steps.title: A pulse and tissue perfusion are different observations
steps.text:
A palpable pulse is a pressure wave travelling through a sufficiently patent artery. It tells you something about that large vessel at that point. It does not directly measure oxygen delivery to each muscle, nerve or patch of skin farther downstream.

For example, increased pressure inside a muscle compartment can impair small-vessel perfusion while a high-pressure artery still carries a pulse. Conversely, anatomical variation can make a particular surface pulse difficult to locate. Use pulses as part of the vascular picture and keep the arterial route separate from the final capillary exchange.

check.q: Why can an arterial pulse remain present while muscle perfusion in a tight compartment is impaired?
check.a: The high-pressure artery can remain open after pressure has compromised the smaller vessels supplying the tissue.

title: The veins of the limbs
summary: Two systems, one set of valves, and the pump that makes it all work.
objectives: Distinguish the superficial from the deep venous system
Explain how the calf muscle pump and the valves return blood against gravity
Account for varicose veins and for deep vein thrombosis anatomically
Trace the route of a venous embolus from the leg to the pulmonary arteries
takeaways: Superficial veins lie in the subcutaneous fat; deep veins accompany the arteries; perforators join them, with valves directing flow inwards.
The great saphenous vein runs in front of the medial malleolus — reliable enough for a surgical cut-down.
Incompetent valves make the superficial system carry pressure it was not built for: varicose veins.
Material leaving a deep leg vein passes through the IVC, right atrium and right ventricle before entering the pulmonary arteries.

steps.title: Two systems and the rule that connects them
steps.text:
Limb veins run in two layers. Superficial veins lie in the subcutaneous fat, outside the deep fascia, and have no muscle around them. Deep veins accompany the arteries inside the fascia, often as paired venae comitantes wrapped round the artery so that arterial pulsation helps drive them.

Perforating veins connect the two, piercing the deep fascia, and their valves allow flow only from superficial to deep. That one-way rule is what the whole system depends on.

check.q: In which direction do the valves of the perforating veins allow flow?
check.a: From superficial to deep.

steps.title: The muscle pump
steps.text:
Standing still, the column of blood from the right atrium to the ankle would exert about 90 mmHg on the veins of the foot. Walking drops that pressure to around 20.

The reason is the calf muscle pump: soleus and gastrocnemius squeeze the deep veins with every step, and the valves ensure the blood can only go upwards. Add the perforator valves keeping superficial blood moving inwards, and the leg empties itself with each stride. Stop walking — a long flight, a hospital bed — and the pump stops with you.

check.q: Which muscle is the main calf pump, and where do the thrombi that follow its failure usually begin?
check.a: Soleus — in its venous sinuses.

steps.title: The great saphenous vein
steps.text:
The longest vein in the body. It begins at the medial end of the dorsal venous arch of the foot, passes in front of the medial malleolus, runs up the medial side of the leg and thigh with the saphenous nerve, and finally dives through the saphenous opening to join the femoral vein.

Its position at the ankle is constant enough to be found by incision in a shocked patient with no visible veins — the classic saphenous cut-down. It is also the vein harvested for coronary bypass, and reversed so its valves do not obstruct.
steps.pitfall: The saphenous nerve travels with the vein below the knee: strip the vein carelessly and the patient is left with a numb medial leg.

steps.title: The small saphenous vein
steps.text:
From the lateral end of the dorsal venous arch, the small saphenous vein passes behind the lateral malleolus, runs up the midline of the calf with the sural nerve, and pierces the deep fascia to join the popliteal vein.

Its termination is variable — sometimes high in the thigh, sometimes into the great saphenous — which is why varicose vein surgery here is done with ultrasound marking rather than from a textbook picture.

steps.title: When the valves fail
steps.text:
If the valves of the saphenofemoral junction or of the perforators become incompetent, blood is pushed outwards into the superficial system with every calf contraction. Those veins are unsupported by fascia, so they dilate and lengthen: varicose veins.

Sustained venous hypertension around the ankle — the gaiter area, where the perforators are — produces the characteristic sequence of oedema, haemosiderin staining, lipodermatosclerosis and finally a venous ulcer, typically over the medial malleolus.

check.q: Why do venous ulcers form around the medial malleolus?
check.a: It is the gaiter area, where incompetent perforators transmit the highest venous pressure to the skin.

steps.title: The arm, briefly
steps.text:
The upper limb repeats the plan. Cephalic vein laterally, up the arm and through the deltopectoral groove into the axillary vein; basilic vein medially, piercing the deep fascia to become the axillary vein; and the median cubital vein joining them across the cubital fossa.

The median cubital vein is the standard site for venepuncture — large, superficial, and separated from the brachial artery and median nerve by the bicipital aponeurosis, the 'grace of God' fascia.

check.q: What protects the brachial artery from a needle in the cubital fossa?
check.a: The bicipital aponeurosis.

steps.title: Follow a clot in the direction of the valves
steps.text:
Imagine a fragment detaching from a thrombus in a deep leg vein. It travels with venous return through progressively larger veins to the inferior vena cava, then the right atrium, tricuspid valve and right ventricle.

The next route is through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries, where a fragment can lodge as the vessels narrow. It does not normally enter the aorta directly because the pulmonary circulation lies between right and left heart. A right-to-left communication can create an exceptional route, but the ordinary anatomy leads towards the lungs.

check.q: Why does an embolus from a deep leg vein usually threaten the lungs rather than travel straight to the brain?
check.a: Normal venous return reaches the right heart and then the pulmonary arterial tree before it can reach the left heart and systemic arteries.

title: The abdominal aorta and its branches
summary: Three unpaired gut arteries, three paired ones, and the levels that let you name a vessel from a CT slice.
objectives: List the branches of the abdominal aorta with their vertebral levels
Explain the difference between the unpaired midline and paired lateral branches
Say why an abdominal aortic aneurysm is usually infrarenal
Explain the asymmetric courses of the renal arteries and veins around the aorta and IVC
takeaways: Coeliac trunk T12, superior mesenteric L1, renal L1/2, inferior mesenteric L3, bifurcation L4.
Unpaired anterior branches supply the gut; paired lateral branches supply the body wall and the urogenital organs.
The aorta ends at L4, at the level of the highest point of the iliac crest.
The right renal artery crosses behind the IVC; the left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta, usually beneath the SMA.

steps.title: From the diaphragm to L4
steps.text:
The aorta enters the abdomen through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12, runs down slightly to the left of the midline on the front of the vertebral bodies, and divides into the two common iliac arteries at L4 — the level of the highest point of the iliac crest.

Because it lies against the vertebral bodies, you can compress it against them in an emergency, and you can feel an aneurysm pulsating through the abdominal wall in a thin patient.

check.q: At which vertebral level does the aorta bifurcate?

steps.title: Three unpaired branches for the gut
steps.text:
The gut hangs from the midline and takes its blood from midline branches, each supplying one embryological division.

Coeliac trunk at T12 — the foregut, to the second part of the duodenum. Superior mesenteric artery at L1 — the midgut, to two thirds of the way along the transverse colon. Inferior mesenteric artery at L3 — the hindgut, to the upper rectum. Each also brings the gut's autonomic plexus and its lymphatics with it.

check.q: Which artery supplies the midgut, and where does its territory end?
check.a: The superior mesenteric artery, ending two thirds of the way along the transverse colon.

steps.title: Paired branches for everything else
steps.text:
The paired branches supply structures that are themselves paired: the inferior phrenic arteries to the diaphragm, the middle suprarenal arteries, the renal arteries at L1/2, and the gonadal arteries.

The gonadal arteries are the giveaway of embryology: they arise high, at L2, because the gonads develop on the posterior abdominal wall and descend later, dragging their blood supply with them. Four pairs of lumbar arteries supply the body wall, and the small median sacral artery continues from the bifurcation.

check.q: Why do the gonadal arteries arise so high on the aorta?
check.a: The gonads develop high on the posterior abdominal wall and descend, taking their arteries with them.

steps.title: Reading a CT slice by level
steps.text:
The levels turn an axial slice into a map. At T12 the coeliac trunk is a short stub dividing into three. At L1 the superior mesenteric artery appears as a circle surrounded by fat, in front of the aorta. Just below, the left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta and under the superior mesenteric artery to reach the inferior vena cava.

That last relationship is why the left renal vein can be compressed between the two vessels — the nutcracker phenomenon — and why the left testicular vein, which drains into it, is the one that gives a varicocele.

check.q: Why is a varicocele usually on the left?
check.a: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at a right angle, which can be compressed under the superior mesenteric artery.

steps.title: Aneurysm
steps.text:
Most abdominal aortic aneurysms are infrarenal. The wall there has fewer vasa vasorum and less elastin than the thoracic aorta, and the reflected pressure wave from the bifurcation adds mechanical stress.

They are usually silent until they leak, when the pain is felt in the back or flank because that is where the blood tracks retroperitoneally. Repair, open or endovascular, is far easier when the aneurysm neck is below the renal arteries — which is one more reason the level matters.
steps.clinical: Back pain, hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass in an older smoker is a leaking aneurysm until proved otherwise.

check.q: Why are most aortic aneurysms below the renal arteries?
check.a: The infrarenal wall has less elastin and fewer vasa vasorum, and takes the reflected pressure wave from the bifurcation.

steps.title: A left-sided artery and a right-sided vein
steps.text:
The aorta lies left of the midline and the inferior vena cava lies to its right. Consequently the right renal artery has farther to travel and passes behind the IVC on its way to the right kidney.

Venous return reverses the asymmetry: the left renal vein crosses towards the right, usually in front of the aorta and behind the superior mesenteric artery. The left renal vein also commonly receives the left gonadal and suprarenal veins. Use the positions of the two great vessels to predict which renal vessel must cross the midline.

check.q: Which renal vessel usually passes anterior to the aorta, and which passes posterior to the IVC?
check.a: The left renal vein passes anterior to the aorta; the right renal artery passes posterior to the IVC.

title: How a blood vessel is built
summary: Three coats, and the way their proportions change tells you the vessel's job.
objectives: Name the three layers of a vessel wall and their contents
Distinguish an elastic artery, a muscular artery, an arteriole, a capillary and a vein under the microscope
Explain the Windkessel effect
Explain why large vessels require vasa vasorum to nourish their own walls
takeaways: Tunica intima, media and adventitia — in every vessel except the capillary.
Elastic arteries store energy in systole and release it in diastole; muscular arteries distribute and regulate.
Veins have thin walls, wide lumens, valves and most of the blood volume.
Diffusion from luminal blood serves the inner wall; vasa vasorum nourish the outer wall of large vessels.

steps.title: Three coats
steps.text:
Tunica intima: a single layer of endothelium on a basement membrane, with a little subendothelial connective tissue. Tunica media: smooth muscle and elastin, arranged circularly. Tunica adventitia: collagen, with the nerves and the vasa vasorum that feed the outer wall of large vessels.

The endothelium is not a passive lining. It controls tone through nitric oxide, controls clotting, and controls which white cells leave the blood. Nearly all vascular disease begins with its failure.

steps.title: Elastic arteries and the Windkessel
steps.text:
The aorta and its great branches have a media packed with concentric elastic lamellae. In systole the wall stretches and stores about half the stroke volume; in diastole it recoils and pushes that blood onwards.

This converts an intermittent pump into a continuous flow — the Windkessel effect. When the elastin degrades with age the aorta stiffens, systolic pressure rises, diastolic falls, and the pulse pressure widens. That is isolated systolic hypertension, and it is a structural change, not a plumbing one.

check.q: Why does pulse pressure widen with age?
check.a: The aorta's elastin degrades, so it cannot store and release the stroke volume — systolic pressure rises and diastolic falls.

steps.title: Muscular arteries and arterioles
steps.text:
Named arteries — radial, femoral, splenic — are muscular: a thick media of smooth muscle between two clear elastic laminae. They distribute blood and adjust it region by region.

Arterioles, with only a few layers of muscle, are the real control point. Because resistance goes as the fourth power of the radius, a small change in arteriolar diameter has an enormous effect: they set both organ blood flow and systemic vascular resistance, and they are what most antihypertensive drugs act on.

check.q: Which vessels set systemic vascular resistance?
check.a: The arterioles.

steps.title: Capillaries
steps.text:
A capillary is endothelium and a basement membrane, and nothing else: about 8 micrometres across, so a red cell must deform to pass. There are three kinds. Continuous (muscle, brain — the blood–brain barrier), fenestrated (gut, endocrine glands, glomerulus — where filtration or rapid exchange is needed) and sinusoidal (liver, spleen, marrow — wide, leaky, with gaps big enough for cells).

The structure follows the job exactly: you can predict the capillary type from what the organ has to do.

check.q: Which capillary type would you expect in the renal glomerulus, and why?
check.a: Fenestrated — it exists to filter.

steps.title: Veins
steps.text:
Compared with its artery, a vein has a thin media, a wide and often collapsed lumen, and a relatively thick adventitia. Around two thirds of the circulating volume sits in the venous system at any moment: it is a reservoir as much as a return path.

Veins below the heart carry valves, paired semilunar cusps of intima, which make flow one-way. Venoconstriction shifts blood from that reservoir back to the heart, which is a large part of how the body compensates for haemorrhage before the blood pressure ever falls.

check.q: Roughly what proportion of the blood volume is in the veins at any moment?
check.a: About two thirds.

steps.title: The wall needs a blood supply of its own
steps.text:
Blood inside a vessel does not automatically nourish every part of its wall. Oxygen and nutrients diffuse from the lumen over only a limited distance. In a thick aortic wall, the outer layers are too far from luminal blood to rely on diffusion alone.

Small vessels called vasa vasorum enter from the adventitia and supply the outer wall of large arteries and veins. The inner wall receives more directly from the lumen. A vessel can therefore contain blood and still have a vulnerable wall if its own small-vessel supply is impaired.

check.q: Why does the aorta need vasa vasorum despite containing oxygenated blood?
check.a: Its wall is too thick for diffusion from the lumen to meet the needs of all the outer layers.
